name: Liam Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Liam. I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter for a big housebuilder on the Oakfield Park estate, three hundred new homes on the edge of town. I do first fix, which is the bones of the house: roof trusses, floor joists, stud walls, and lately fitting the stairs. Steve, the carpentry foreman, gives me a plot number and a list at seven, and I'm usually behind by three. The houses are all one of five designs, so you get to know them like your own kitchen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay's good, we're on a price per plot and the firm pays above the going rate to keep people. The hard part is I'm not quick enough yet, the older lads do a staircase in half the time. My dad was a joiner back in Poland and he could do a stair by eye, so it bugs me. Ana, my girlfriend, says I'm too hard on myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that it's good news for anyone who actually builds things. At work the lads would joke about it for a week. I don't really post stuff, maybe a comment on the football group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. Houses still need building, there are three big estates going up within twenty minutes of here, and we're short of carpenters, not of computers. What's on my mind is getting quicker and getting my wedding paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on Oakfield and get my stairs time down. Ana and I are getting married at St Joseph's in the spring, and that's paid for already out of savings. My brother Piotr and I own two lock-up garages we rent out, and I'd buy a third one this year if the one on Mill Road comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things are on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the garages.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dad bought the first one before he died, to keep his van in. Piotr and I bought a second one together and now we rent both out for storage, it's about a hundred and fifty a month each. It's not big money, but it's ours. My dad always said own something, even if it's small, so my brother and I rent out two lock-up garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ana's work change in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She was a receptionist at a dental practice and she's training to be a dental nurse now. She wanted to be with the patients, not on the phone. In AI Plateau nothing much changes for her either, maybe the booking gets a bit easier.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for anyone who **builds things**.
The lads would **joke** about it for a week, and I'd maybe comment on the football group.
think: **Three big estates** are going up nearby, and we're short of **carpenters**.
What's on my mind is **getting quicker** and the **wedding**.
do: Keep working on Oakfield and cut my **stairs time** down.
Marry Ana at **St Joseph's** in the spring, already paid from savings.
Buy a **third lock-up garage** on Mill Road if it comes up.
S0.quote: My dad always said own something, even if it's small, so my brother and I rent out two lock-up garages.
fieldNote: His cushion includes **rented garages** owned with his brother, following his late dad's advice.
He measures himself against his dad, a **joiner in Poland**.
Ana's move to **dental nursing** already shields the household.

steps.text: Cut his staircase fitting time on the Oakfield plots
Marry Ana at St Joseph's in the spring
Buy a third lock-up garage on Mill Road with his brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change the office, not the site, at least for now. I'd tell people the trades are a good bet for young lads, better than a desk. I'd probably say that at the pub more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd watch the firm. They've already got an app where the site manager snaps a photo of a plot and it lists the snags, the bits that need fixing. If AI does the planning, buying and booking, there are fewer people in the sales office, but the housebuilder still needs me to put the roof on. Ana got out of reception just in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the snag app properly, since Steve says it'll come to carpenters next year, and I'd rather be first than last. I'd put a bit more into savings each month, maybe a hundred. Otherwise keep going: wedding, garages, getting quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be first than last with the app. Is that like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not usually. I wait till the other lads try things. But Steve's a good foreman and if he says it's coming, it's coming. I'd rather learn it on a quiet Friday than have it forced on me with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lady in the sales office, Carol, who does the bookings for the buyers' viewings. She's lovely and she's been there since the estate started. If a computer books the viewings and answers the emails, I don't know what she does. I'd worry about her more than me.

say: AI will change the **office, not the site**, at least for now.
I'd tell people the **trades** are a better bet for young lads than a **desk**.
think: The firm already has a **snag app** that lists faults from a photo.
Fewer people in the **site cabin**, but they still need me for the **roof**.
do: Learn the **snag app** properly before it reaches carpenters next year.
Put an extra **hundred** a month into savings.
Carry on with the **wedding**, garages and getting quicker.
S1.quote: If AI does the planning, buying and booking, there are fewer people in the sales office, but the housebuilder still needs me to put the roof on.
fieldNote: He sees the hit in the **office** first, matching his hands-on job.
He'd adopt the **snag app** early because a trusted foreman says it's coming.
Ana's switch to **dental nursing** lowers the household risk.

steps.text: Learn the snag app before it reaches carpenters
Put an extra hundred a month into savings
Keep fitting stairs and roofs on the Oakfield estate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and that families will need to pull together. I don't trust the government to fix it, so I'd say look after your own. I'd say it to the lads at the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for me. Our houses are five designs repeated three hundred times, which is exactly what a robot can learn. The AI takes the office in 2028, and by 2031 the robots could put up trusses and stairs. I'd be thirty-one with a new wife and maybe a baby, and I'd be out of the one thing I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for whatever course trains people to run and fix the site robots, because I'd rather be on the machine than replaced by it. I'd stop the third garage and keep the money in the bank. Ana and I would keep the wedding small and hold off on a baby for a bit, which would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the garages and savings, but I can see the end of my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the AI. What does that mean for you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got three years of plots left and I should use them. I'd work every Saturday to pile up money. And I'd watch the firm, because the moment they buy one robot for one plot, the writing's on the wall for all three hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned holding off on a baby. How would that conversation go with Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. She's wanted a family since we met, and so have I, it's how we were both raised. I'd say a year, two at most, until I know where I'll be working. She'd say her nursing job is safer than mine now, and she'd be right, which is a funny thing to admit.

say: It's a **shock**, and **families** will need to pull together.
I don't trust the **government**, so I'd say look after your **own**.
think: Five designs repeated **three hundred times** is exactly what a robot can learn.
By **2031** I'd be thirty-one with a new wife, out of the **one thing** I know.
do: Sign up for a course to **run and fix** site robots.
Drop the **third garage** and keep the money in the bank.
Keep the wedding small and **hold off** on a baby for a year or two.
feel: **Anxious**, with a cushion but seeing the end of his **trade**.
S2.quote: Our houses are five designs repeated three hundred times, which is exactly what a robot can learn.
fieldNote: He clearly sees **volume housebuilding** as robot-friendly because it repeats.
The **three-year gap** becomes Saturday work and a robot course.
Delaying a **baby** is the cost that hurts him most, and Ana's job is now safer.

steps.text: Enrol on a course to run and fix site robots
Skip the third garage and keep the cash saved
Hold off on a baby for a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, and that apprenticeships and family firms are how you do it. Young lads should learn a real trade, but a specialist one. I'd keep saying the same at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2034 gives me eight years of first fix, and by then I'd be decent at stairs. Stairs on these estates are all the same, so the robot gets those too. But the old houses and the one-off stairs, curved ones and oak ones, those are different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Steve to put me on every stair he can, then take an evening course in bespoke joinery, making one-off stairs and doors. In a few years I'd talk to Piotr about using the garage savings for a small joinery workshop. We'd have the wedding as planned and try for a baby in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bespoke joinery specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what my dad did. My dad made a curved oak stair for a church in our old town, and I've got a photo of it on my phone. A robot made for three hundred identical houses isn't going to do that. Maybe it will one day, but not soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the workshop a big risk with a baby on the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes. But Piotr would go halves, and the garages bring in money every month. I wouldn't quit Oakfield until the workshop had real orders. That's how Dad would have done it, careful.

say: There's time to **prepare**, through apprenticeships and **family firms**.
Young lads should learn a **specialist trade**, and I'd keep saying so at the pub.
think: Robots around **2034** leave me eight years of first fix.
Estate stairs go to robots, but **one-off stairs** in oak are different.
do: Ask Steve for **every stair** going on the estate.
Take an evening course in **bespoke joinery**.
Plan a small **joinery workshop** with Piotr using the garage savings.
S3.quote: My dad made a curved oak stair for a church in our old town, and I've got a photo of it on my phone.
fieldNote: He moves toward **bespoke joinery**, echoing his late father's work.
Five years keeps the **baby** plan on track, unlike the fast picture.
His plans are **careful**: no quitting until the workshop has real orders.

steps.text: Take an evening course in bespoke joinery
Open a small joinery workshop with his brother
Try for a baby with Ana in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and there's no excuse for anyone not to plan. Learn a proper trade, save and look after your family. Same as I always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2039 I'd be forty with thirteen years of carpentry. I'd hope to be a foreman or running my own joinery work by then. Foremen do a lot of planning, which AI takes in 2036, but someone still has to stand on site and sort the lads out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Oakfield, get quick, and go for foreman in five years or so. Buy the third garage when it comes up. Marry Ana and start a family when we planned. Maybe learn the bespoke joinery later, as a side line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal life with a storm a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you use AI in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as the firm brings it in. I'd use the snag app, the ordering app, whatever they give us, once the other lads have tried it. I'm not one to go hunting for new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your kids in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to learn to make something with their hands, like my dad and me, even if a robot does most of it by then. It teaches you patience. And I'd want them to own something, like Dad said.

say: **Ten years** is fair warning, so there's **no excuse** not to plan.
Learn a **proper trade**, save and look after your family, as I always say.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty, hopefully a **foreman** or doing my own joinery.
AI takes foremen's **planning** in 2036, but someone still sorts the lads out on site.
do: Go for **foreman** at Oakfield in about five years.
Buy the **third garage** when it comes up.
Start a **family** with Ana when planned, and learn bespoke joinery later.
feel: **Calm**, a normal life with a **storm far off**.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to learn to make something with their hands, like my dad and me, even if a robot does most of it by then.
fieldNote: With a decade, he returns to his **steady** path: foreman, garages, family.
He knows **foreman work** includes planning AI will take.
He'd use AI tools **once others** have tried them, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Work towards foreman on the housebuilding estate
Buy the third lock-up garage with his brother
Start a family with Ana on the planned timeline

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Robots on identical estates by 2031, just when we'd want a baby. What would help is the housebuilders paying for carpenters to train on the robots or in specialist joinery, a proper apprenticeship for grown men, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it means for my dad's trade. He came here to work with wood, and I followed him. If robots do all the woodwork, something gets lost that money doesn't replace.

headlineQuote: If robots do all the woodwork, something gets lost that money doesn't replace.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old junior carpenter** doing first fix on a large new-build housing estate.
With his brother he owns **two rented garages**, and he has savings and a paid-for **wedding**.
Traditional and Catholic, he trusts **family and trade** over government help.
He adopts tech **once proven** and would move to **bespoke joinery**, like his late father.
He is **anxious** in the fast picture, fearing robots on identical estates, and calm with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots on identical estates by 2031, just as he'd want a **baby**.
whatWouldHelp: Housebuilders paying for **adult apprenticeships** in robots or **specialist joinery**, not handouts.
